name: Fatima Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Happy to. I'm Fatima, 27, and I'm in my second year as an apprentice lineworker with the city's electricity company. I share a flat near the ring road with my friend Priya, who tests software for a bank.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. Then let's start simple. Walk me through a normal working day for you.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now our crew is upgrading the lines that feed a new data centre park on the north edge of the city. We're swapping old wire for thicker cable and fitting sensors on the poles that report faults back to the control room. The grid has to double for all these data centres, and somebody has to build it. For the next few years, that somebody is me. My foreman Gus lets me run the sensor setup on the tablet, because I'm the one who doesn't swear at it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: So you're comfortable with the tech side?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: More than comfortable. I use AI every day, to study for my exams, to turn my scribbled notes into proper job logs, and to ask about any fault I don't understand. I'm not a strong climber yet, so I make up for it with homework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. A bit of an anticlimax, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are useful but they're not magic, which is what I'd been saying anyway. I'd keep showing the crew the handy bits. Online I'd shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, and that's fine. The data centres still need power, so the work keeps coming. My job is safe and my pay goes up when I qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my second-year exams by summer and keep saving about 200 a month. I'd start saving for a drone pilot course, because inspection drones are already being used and I like the idea. Otherwise, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already on your mind about money or work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I've got about five months of bills saved, rent's split with Priya, and the work is steady. My mum worries I'll fall off a pole, but that's a separate thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use AI as much in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. I use AI every day to study, and in this picture it stays a clever notebook. I can live with a clever notebook.

I'd keep showing the **crew** the handy bits of the tablet.
think: **Data centres** still need power, so the work keeps coming.
My job is **safe**, and pay rises when I qualify.
do: Save about **200 a month**, partly toward a drone pilot course.
Keep using AI **daily** for study and job logs.
feel: **Calm**, with a little disappointment at the anticlimax.

fieldNote: Her confidence rests on **grid demand** from data centres, which keeps crews busy.
She compensates for weak **climbing** with study and tech skill.
Already eyeing **drone inspection** as a next step even with nothing changing.

steps.text: Finish second-year line exams by summer
Keep using AI daily for study and job logs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels close. Some of that is already happening around me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say line work is one of the safer trades, and I'd tell people to look at apprenticeships. I'd also say people need help switching, because not everyone can just pick up a new skill. I'd post my study setup for other apprentices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for my job and bad for my flat. Line crews get busier, but the people around me with desk jobs get squeezed. That's where my worry sits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gus to put me forward for the AI fault-finding trial and be the crew's go-to person. I'd ask the company to pay for a drone pilot licence, about 1,200, as part of my training. And I'd push savings to 300 a month in case Priya moves out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my work, but for the people I live and hang out with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Priya tests software. Does this picture touch her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Priya tests software for a living, and that's exactly the job AI eats first. If Priya moves out, my rent doubles overnight. I'd have to find another flatmate or move further out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your own crew change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The control room would get smarter, so we'd get sent straight to the right pole instead of driving the whole line. Less patrolling, more fixing. I'd love that, honestly.

People switching careers need **real help**, not just advice.
think: This is **good for my job** and bad for my flat.
Friends with **desk jobs** get squeezed while my crew gets busier.
do: Ask Gus for a place on the **fault-finding trial**.
Get the company to fund a **drone licence**, about 1,200.
Raise savings to **300 a month** in case Priya moves out.
feel: **Uneasy** for friends, while her **own work** feels fine.

fieldNote: Her exposure runs through the **shared rent**, not her own job.

steps.text: Join the AI fault-finding trial through foreman Gus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Oof. That's faster than I'd want, even me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need fast, paid retraining, not leaflets. I'd say the company should train its own crews to run the robots, not hire new people. I'd post that, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years isn't enough time to retrain anybody properly. I'd be learning to supervise robots on YouTube at night while still climbing poles by day. I think there'll be robot supervisor jobs, but far fewer than there are lineworkers now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the robotics maintenance course at the technical college straight away, two evenings a week. I'd apply to the company's inspection or automation team the minute it opened. I'd save everything I could, about 400 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd have a plan, but the plan has fewer seats than people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and robots around 2031. How does that split land for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the control room and the planning change overnight, which I'd actually like. Then by 2031 the robot crews come, and the question is whether I'm running them or watching them. Three years is just about long enough if I start the day the news breaks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're usually the keen one. What's different here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being keen doesn't help if there are ten of us for every robot supervisor job. I'm good with tech but I'm still a junior. Someone with fifteen years on the lines will get picked first.

fieldNote: Even this **early adopter** sees the job numbers shrinking at robot arrival.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's workable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this well, so let's not waste it arguing. I'd keep pushing the company to train its own people first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, I'd be the woman with the drone licence and the robot ticket before anyone else on my crew had heard of either. I'd be qualified, with a few years in, and right at the front of the line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify in 2028, get the drone licence that year, then do the robotics course from 2029. I'd move onto the inspection team by 2031. And I'd put a bit into an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a big change, but I'd feel ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does 'robot ticket' mean, for someone outside the trade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A ticket is just what we call a certificate that lets you do a certain job. A robot ticket would be the certificate saying you can set up and supervise a line robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with your savings in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep five months in the bank, then about 100 a month into an index fund, which spreads money across lots of big companies. If robot makers do well, I'd get a little of that.

The company should **train its own** people first.

Being qualified and **early** puts me at the front of the line.

Put about **100 a month** into an index fund.
S3.quote: With five years, I'd be the woman with the drone licence and the robot ticket before anyone else on my crew had heard of either.
fieldNote: Five years lets her **get certified** before the field crowds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Honestly, that sounds like an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone in the trade should start learning now. I'd run little sessions for the apprentices on the tools I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty. By 2039 I'd want to be the one telling the robots where the faults are. I'd be 40, senior, and certified on the new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, work the lines for a few years, and take the drone and robot courses when the company offers them. I'd keep using AI every day and keep a small index fund going. Nothing rushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, even. This is the version where I come out well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The older guys on Gus's crew, the ones in their late forties. They'd be too young to retire in 2039 and too set in their ways to want to learn robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change your life plans at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd finally buy a flat instead of renting with Priya. With ten good years of pay, I could manage a deposit by 2030.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because I'd give up, but because there'd be ten of us for every new job and no time to get ahead. What would help is the company training its own crews to run the robots, paid and in work hours, starting now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people we live with. My job's fairly safe, but my rent depends on a flatmate whose job isn't.

headlineQuote: The grid has to double for all these data centres, and somebody has to build it. For the next few years, that somebody is me.
portrait: Fatima is a 27-year-old **second-year apprentice** upgrading lines for a city data centre park.
She uses **AI daily** to study and write job logs, and makes up for weak climbing with homework.
Her nearest risk is **shared rent** with a flatmate whose software testing job is exposed.
She is anxious at AGI by 2028 because **supervisor jobs** will be few, but calm with ten years.
Her plan runs through a **drone licence** and robot certificates.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with too many crew chasing too few robot jobs.
whatWouldHelp: The company **training its own crews** to run robots, paid and in work hours.
